children: A few weeks ago, Microsoft disclosed a large gain from its investment in OpenAI. Depending on the period being discussed, Microsoft has reported different OpenAI-related impacts: a gain in one period, losses in another, and later a larger full-year benefit. The numbers were real. But they were not a simple answer to the question most readers care about: did Microsoft's own business perform better?

That gap between the headline number and the accounting underneath it is where many earnings stories go wrong. Not because reporters are lazy. Usually, the problem is simpler. Accounting often puts investment gains, valuation changes or one-time items close enough to operating profit that a headline can make them look like ordinary business performance.
Here are four recurring patterns, with one example much closer to Dalal Street than to Redmond.
1. Equity-method accounting: A stake can create profits and losses of its own

First, equity-method accounting and dilution gains. When a company owns roughly 20 to 50% of another business, it usually records its share of that business's profits or losses each period, even if no cash is received. There is also a subtler case. If the investee raises money at a higher valuation, the original investor's ownership percentage can fall even as the value of its stake rises. After OpenAI's 2025 restructuring, Microsoft said its stake in OpenAI Group PBC was valued at about $135 billion, representing about 27% on an as-converted diluted basis. Microsoft also said that, excluding the impact of OpenAI's recent funding rounds, it had previously held 32.5% of the OpenAI for-profit. That is a valuation and restructuring story, not evidence that OpenAI had suddenly become profitable.
2. Mark-to-market gains: When an investment, not the business, drives profit

Second, mark-to-market gains. A similar problem appears when a company holds an investment that is measured at fair value. Amazon's second-quarter 2026 results are a clean example. Net income rose to $62.6 billion, and the company said that figure included $53.4 billion of non-operating pre-tax other income, primarily from its investments in Anthropic. Operating income, which is a better starting point for Amazon's retail, advertising and cloud performance, rose 43%. One number described the business. The other mostly described the valuation of an AI investment.
3. Model-driven gains: Ask where the valuation came from

Third, model-driven gains. Enron is the old warning label. It used mark-to-market accounting for long-term energy contracts, but the marks often came from management's own models rather than prices outsiders could observe. The lesson still holds: when a gain is called mark-to-market, ask one more question. Market price, funding-round price or management model?
4. The Dalal Street version: Info Edge shows how big the gap can get

Fourth, the Indian version. Info Edge, the parent of Naukri.com, has given investors a live case study in how large these effects can be. Info Edge first invested in Zomato in 2010. When Zomato listed in 2021, Info Edge's accounts recorded an unrealised mark-to-market gain of ₹8,941.2 crore on the Zomato investment and a realised gain of ₹357.1 crore from selling shares in the offer for sale. Its net profit for the quarter jumped to ₹7,369.34 crore. That was a very successful investment outcome. It was not a measure of how Naukri, 99acres or the rest of the operating business had suddenly performed.

The pattern has continued. For the year ended March 2026, Info Edge reported standalone net profit of ₹55,357.08 million, or about ₹5,535.7 crore, compared with ₹7,734.20 million the year before. The big driver was not recruitment revenue. It was a ₹52,001.12 million unrealised fair-value gain linked to the reclassification of its Makesense/PB Fintech holding. The same filing also showed large fair-value movements in other comprehensive income, including a ₹91,393.56 million movement for Eternal, formerly Zomato, in the prior-year comparison column. Meanwhile, the standalone business itself had a more normal year: revenue from operations grew 15% and operating profit grew 16.9%.
A good investment is not the same thing as a better business

None of this means Microsoft was wrong to back OpenAI, Amazon was wrong to back Anthropic, or Info Edge was wrong to back Zomato and PB Fintech. These may be excellent investments. The point is that an investment gain answers a different question from operating performance. A headline that blurs the two usually gives readers the more exciting answer, not the more useful one.
Three questions reporters should ask before writing the headline

The fix starts with accounting literacy. Journalists covering earnings do not need to become chartered accountants. But they do need enough accounting knowledge to know when a profit number is doing something unusual. Ask three questions. Is the number operating profit or investment income? Did the gain come from a cash sale or from a valuation change? And if reported profit moves by a multiple that dwarfs revenue or operating-profit growth, what else moved the number?
Read the notes, not just the press release

For journalists who cover this beat often, this should be part of the craft. Start with the notes, not just the press release. The reconciliation tables, fair-value disclosures and related-party notes often contain the sentence that would have changed the headline. Read the cash flow statement alongside the income statement. Learn the handful of accounting traps that recur every quarter: gross versus net revenue, equity-method gains and losses, impairments, fair-value marks and non-GAAP add-backs. And when the filing is moving too fast, call someone who reads accounts for a living. A five-minute check with a practising analyst, accountant or accounting academic can save a headline from turning a valuation mark into a business story.
The businesses may be fine. It is the profit number that needs a second look, preferably from someone trained to read it.
(The author is Kester and Byrnes Professor of Accounting and Auditing at Columbia Business School. Views are personal.)

title: Why journalists should look beyond net profit when covering earnings
